الامتحان السابع: قد استدعيت كلاما في حد الحركة والخائضون فيه ضبطهم
كثير، فقيل انه الذي لمحله به اسم المتحرك، وقيل إنه الذي تكون الذات به
متحركة، وقيل إنه الخروج عن المكان وقد فهمت ما في هذا النمط من فائدة أو
غائلة، فإن أردت الحقيقة فعليك بالمنهج الذي ذللته لك فلم أكرره بالامتحان
مرة بعد أخرى إلا لتألف هذا المسلك البعيد وهو أن تحصل الألفاظ المشهورة
وتضعها  في جانب من ذهنك، وهاهنا ثلاثة: الكون والحركة والسكون، وتنظر في
المعاني المعقولة التي تدل هذه العبارات عليها من غير التفات إلى الألفاظ،
فتقول هذا المنظور فيه من فن الأعراض،
ونحن نعلم أن العرض ينقسم إلى ما يعبر عنه بأنه اختصاص جوهر بحيزه وإلى
ما لا يعبر عنه به. واختصاص الجوهر بحيزه ينقسم بالضرورة إلى ما يكون في
حالة واحدة والى ما يكون فن أكثر. والذي يكون أكثر ينقسم إلى ما يزيد على
حالتين وإلى ما لا يزيد. والذي يكون في حالتين ينقسم إلى ما يكون في حيز
واحد وإلى ما يكون في حيزين، وكذا ما يكون في ثلاثة أحوال فصاعدا ينقسم إلى
ما يكون في حيز واحد وإلى ما يكون في ثلاثة أحياز. فقد حصل هاهنا للعقل
خمسة أقسام كون في حالة وكون في حالتين في حيز واحد وكون في حالتين في
حيزين وكون في ثلاثة أحوال في حيز واحد وكون في ثلاثة أحوال في ثلاثة
احياز. وكانت الألفاظ ثلاثة والأقسام خمسة فاختلف الناس في إطلاق تلك
الألفاظ على هذه الأقسام. فقال فريق وهو الأقرب إلى الحق، واعني بالحق
هاهنا تقريب التعريف والاصطلاح، وإلا فليس في هذا النظم رسم معنوي وإنما هو
بحث عن اللفظ الفاشي يعبر بالسكون عن الاختصاص بحيز في حالتين متواصلتين
فصاعدا، وبالحركة عن الاختصاص بحيزين في حالتين متواصلتين فصاعدا، وهؤلاء
لم يسقوا الجوهر في أول حدوثه لا ساكنا ولا متحركا فثار عليهم من يأخذ
الأمور من بعد. فقال هذا يؤدي إلى أن يكون جوهر غير ساكن ولا متحرك وهذا
محال، والمؤدي إلى المحال محال فسلم الكلام المشهور بين المتكلمين أن
الحركة والسكون يتقابلان لا ينفك الجوهر عنهما. ولم يعرف أن الذين قالوا
ذلك أرادوا به الذي يبقى مدة يدركه الحس، فالثاني لا يخلو عن حركة وسكون
فإنهم فهموا من السكون أشياء، فكيف سموا الاختصاص في الحاة الأولى سكونا،
فإن كان يسمى به باعتبار أنه ليس بمتحرك فليكن متحركا باعتبار أنه ليس
بساكن، أي ليس بلا  لبث، وهذا خوض في فصول بلا طائل بعد معرفة المعنى، وثار
من بعد خيال آخر وهو أن الحركة إن كانت عبارة عن الكون في المكانين فلا
تكون الحركة قط موجودة في حال من الأحوال. لأن الكون في مكانين يكون في
آنين، فإن نظرت إلى ألان الأول فالكون الثاني غير موجود وإن نظرت إلى
الثاني فلا يكون إلا بعد عدم الأول. وهذا كما إن تبذل السواد والبياض لا
يكون موجودا، أعني نفس التبدل لأنه ما دام السواد موجودا فلا تبدل. وإذا
وجد البياض بعد عدم السواد فلا تبدل. فيكون التبدل عبارة أطلقت على أمر
معقول يستدعي ثبوته زيادة على إن واحد. فقالوا الحركة لا وجود لها بالفعل
في آن البتة وإنما وجودها في زمان ممتد، والزمان لا يوجد منه جزء ما لم يفن
الذي قبله، فلا يصادف وجودا إلا في الوهم إما في الخارج فلا. وهؤلاء هم
الفلاسفة. وقال أهل الحق
لسنا نطلق اسم الحركة عليه من حيث انه كونان في مكانين بل من حيث انه كون
في مكان لم يكن قبله وبعده فيه، فألزموا أن الجرم الذي وجد في حالة واحدة
لم يكن قبله ولا بعده فيه فزادوا مع وجود الجوهر للاحتراز. وهذا الإطلاق
يستدعي صدقه ثلاثة أحوال، فمن يكتفي بحالتين وتكون الحركة عنده عبارة عن
كون الجوهر في حيز لم يكن قبله فيه مع وجوده، وأعني به الفصل القريب. فهو
مسمى حركة من حيث أنه شغل بحيز حصل به مع فراغ الآخر. وأما السكون فهو كون
في مكان كان قبله فيه. ومن أراد أن يغير هذه العبارات فلا حجر عليه بعد أن
يقرر في عقله الأقسام الخمسة الأول، فإنه بعد ذلك سنة اللغوي الناظر في
الألفاظ لا المتكلم الباحث عن المعاني. ولنختم الامتحانات بذكر حد واحد من
حدود الفقهاء والأصوليين.
الامتحان الثامن: اختلفوا في حد الواجب فقيل الواجب ما تعلق به الإيجاب،
وقيل ما لا بد من فعله، وقيل ما يثاب على فعله ويعاقب على تركه، وقيل ما
يجب  بتركه العقاب، وقيل ما لا يجوز الإقدام على تركه، وقيل ما يصير المكتف
بتركه عاصيا، وقيل ما يلام تاركه شرعا. ولو تتبعت هذه الحدود طال الأمر
ففيما قدمته ما يعرفك وجه الخلل في المختل منها، لكن أهديك إلى الحق الواضح
بتمهيد سبيل السلوك، وهو أن تستنهج ما نهجته لك فتعلم أن الألفاظ في هذا
الفن خمسة الواجب والمحظور والمندوب والمكروه والمباح. فدع الألفاظ جانبا
وجز بالنظر إلى المعنى أولا، وأنت تعلم أن الواجب اسم مشترك، إذ يطلقه
المتكلم في مقابلة الممتنع، ويقول
وجود الله واجب، واللغوي على السقوط يقول وجبت جنوبها ويقول وجبت الشمس،
فله بكل اعتبار حد آخر. والمطلب ألان مراد الفقهاء، وهذه الألفاظ لا نشك
أنها لا تطلق على الجواهر بل على الأعراض، ومن الأعراض على الأفعال فقط،
ومن الأفعال على أفعال المكلفين لا أفعال البهائم. فإذا نظرك إلى أقسام
الفعل لا من حيث كونه مقدورا أو حادثا أو معلوما أو مكتسبا أو مخترعا، وله
بحسب كل نسبة انقسامات، إذ عوارض الأفعال ولوازمها كثيرة فلا ننظر فيها،
ولكن إطلاق هذا الاسم عليها من حيث نسبتها إلى خطاب الشرع يعلم أن الأفعال
تنقسم إلى ما لا يتعلق بها خطاب الشرع كأفعال البهائم والمجانين والى ما
يتعلق به، والذي يتعلق به ينقسم إلى ما تعلق به على وجه التخيير والتسوية
بين الإقدام عليه والإحجام عنه، ويسمى مباحا، وإلى ما رجح فعله على تركه،
وإلى ما رجح تركه على فعله. والذي رجح فعله على تركه ينقسم إلى ما أشعر
بأنه لا عقاب على تركه ويسمى مندوبا وإلى ما أشعر بأنه يعاقب على تركه في
الدار الآخرة ويسمى واجبا. وربما اصطلح فريق على تخصيص الواجب بما علم
ترجيحه على هذا الوجه قطعا كالصلوات الخمس المكتوبة دون ما هو مخير فيه،
وخصصوا ذاك باسم الفرض ولا حرج في هذا الاصطلاح، فإننا لا ننكر انقسام
المرجح بالعقاب إلى المعلوم والمظنون والاصطلاح مباح فلا مشاحة فيه. وأما
المرجح تركه فينقسم إلى ما أشعر بأنه لا  عقاب على فعله ويسقى مكروها، وقد
تكرر ما أشعر عليه بعقاب في الدنيا، كما قال عليه السلام إما يخشى الذي
يرفع رأسه قبل الإمام أن يحول الله رأسه رأس حمار. وقوله من نام بعد العصر
فاختلس عقله فلا يلومن إلا نفسه.
وإلى ما أشعر بعقاب في الآخرة على فعله وهو المسمى محذورا أو حراما أو
معصية، فإن قلت ما معنى قولك أشعر، فمعناه أنه عرف بدلالة من خطاب صريح
أو قرينة أو معنى مستنبط أو فعل أو إشارة. فالإشعار يعم جميع المدارك، فان
قلت ما معنى قولك عليه عقاب فمعناه أن إجرائه سبب للعقاب في الآخرة، فان
قلت ما المراد بكونه سببآ فالمراد ما يفهم من. قولنا اسل سبب الشبع وحز
الرقبة سبب الموت والضرب سبب الألم، فان قلت فلو كان سببا لكان لا يرجى
العفو بل كان يجب أن يعاقب لا محالة. فأقول ليس كذلك إذ لا يفهم من قولنا
الضرب سبب الألم والدواء سبب الشفاء أن ذلك واجب في كل شخص معين مشار إليه،
بل يجوز أن يفرض في المحل أمور تدفع المسبب، ولا يدل ذلك على بطلان
السببية، فرب دواء لا ينفع ورب ضرب لا يدرك المضروب ألمه لكونه مشغول النفس
بأمر هام، كمن يجرح في حال قتال وهو لا يحس في الحال به، وكما أن العلة قد
تستحكم فتدفع أثر الدواء فكذلك قد يكون في سريرة الشخص وباطنه أخلاق رضية
وخصال محمودة عند الله مرضية يوجب ذلك العفو عن جريمته ولا يوجب خروج
الجريمة عن كونها سبب العقاب.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح د د (ḥ-d-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Literally "to prevent, restrain, hinder" — a boundary that bars entry or exit; the limit that demarcates one thing from another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, the "definition" (ḥadd) is that which intellectually circumscribes the quiddity (māhīyah) of a thing, distinguishing it from all else.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The literal sense is physical prevention (manʿ); the logical sense is a metaphorical extension (istiʿārah) — the definition "prevents" confusion by delimiting the essence.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Mushtarak (Homonymy) — When a single lexical form (lafẓ) applies to multiple distinct realities (ḥaqāʾiq), each referent requires its own definition; disagreement presupposes a shared subject (tawārud), which is absent in cases of pure homonymy.
chapters.translation:
I say: The First Examination. People have differed concerning the definition of definition (ḥadd al-ḥadd). One group says: "The definition of a thing is its reality (ḥaqīqah), its very self (nafs), and its essence (dhāt)." Another group says: "The definition of a thing is the utterance (lafẓ) that explicates its meaning in a manner that combines (jāmiʿ) and prevents (māniʿ)." A third group supposes this to be a genuine point of contention and champions one of the two definitions over the other. Observe how the intellect of this third party has become entangled! For they failed to realize that disagreement is only conceivable after the disputants have converged upon a single subject (tawārud ʿalā shayʾ wāḥid). Yet these two [definitions] have diverged and distanced themselves from one another; they never converged. The source of this error is nothing but heedlessness (dhuhūl) regarding the knowledge of the homonymous name (al-ism al-mushtarak) which we have already mentioned.

For he who defines the "free agent" (mukhtār) as "one who has power over both abandoning and performing a thing" is not opposing him who defines it as "one who has been left to his own opinion (khallā wa raʾyih)." Likewise, he who defines "eye" (ʿayn) as "the organ that perceives colors by sight" does not contradict him who defines "eye" as "the metallic substance that is the noblest of coins." Rather, the latter has defined a matter entirely distinct from the reality of the other. They merely share the name "eye" and "free agent." Understand this, for it is a principle (qānūn) of great benefit.

If you say: "What then is correct in your view concerning the definition of definition?" — Know that he who seeks meanings from utterances is lost and ruined, like one who turns his back to the West while seeking it. But he who first establishes the meanings in his mind without any utterance, and then makes the utterances follow the meanings, has been rightly guided. Let us then establish the meanings. We say: A thing has four ranks (marātib) in existence. The first is its reality in itself (ḥaqīqah fī nafsih). The second is the fixing of an image (mithāl) of its reality in the mind — this is what is expressed as knowledge (ʿilm). The third is the composition of its image with letters that signify it — this is the expression (ʿibārah) indicating the image present in the soul. The fourth is the composition of script (ruqūm) perceived by the sense of sight, signifying the utterance — this is writing (kitābah). Writing follows utterance, for it signifies it; utterance follows knowledge, for it indicates it; and knowledge follows the known, for it corresponds and conforms to it. These four are concordant, mutually conforming, and balanced. However, the first two are true existences (wujūdān ḥaqīqiyyān) that do not vary across epochs, whereas the latter two — utterance and writing — vary across epochs and nations, for they are posited by convention (waḍʿ bi-al-ikhtiyār). But although the conventions differ in their forms, they agree in being posited with the intent of conforming to reality.

Now, it is known that "definition" (ḥadd) is derived from "prevention" (manʿ), and it is only metaphorically applied to these meanings due to their sharing in the sense of prevention. So consider where you find it among these four. If you begin with the reality, you will not doubt that it encompasses the thing and is exclusive to it, for the reality of each thing is its particular property (khāṣṣiyyah) which belongs to it and to no other. Thus the reality is comprehensive and preventive (jāmiʿah māniʿah). If you then look at the image of the reality in the mind — namely knowledge — you find it likewise, for it conforms to the preventive reality. Conformity necessitates participation in prevention. If you look at the expression of knowledge, you find it also encompassing, for it conforms to the knowledge that conforms to the reality; and that which conforms to that which conforms is itself conforming. If you look at writing, you find it conforming to the utterance that conforms to the knowledge that conforms to the reality — so it too is conforming. Thus prevention is found in all four, except that custom (ʿādah) does not run to applying the name "definition" to writing, which is the fourth, nor to knowledge, which is the second. Rather, it is shared (mushtarak) between two realities. Therefore, it must have two different definitions, like the word "eye" and "free agent" and their analogues.

So when applied to the thing itself, the definition of definition is: the reality of the thing and its essence. And upon the second application, the definition of definition is: the utterance that is comprehensive and preventive. However, those who apply it to the utterance also differ in their conventions, as we mentioned concerning the verbal (lafẓī), the descriptive (rasmī), and the real (ḥaqīqī) definitions. Thus, the definition of definition for him who is satisfied with mere repetition of the word — such as saying "existence is thingness," "motion is transference," "knowledge is cognition" — is: the substitution of an utterance for what is already present to the questioner, under the condition that it combines and prevents. As for the definition of definition for him who is satisfied with descriptive definitions (rusūm), it is: the utterance that explicates a word by enumerating its essential and necessary attributes in a manner that distinguishes it from others with a distinction that is coextensive (ṭard) and converse (ʿaks). As for its definition for him who applies the name "definition" only to the real definition, it is: the statement (qawl) that indicates the complete quiddity (tamām māhīyah) of a thing. In this, there is no need to mention coextension and converse, for that follows the quiddity necessarily; nor does one attend to the necessary or the accidental, for only the essential (dhātiyyāt) indicate the quiddity.

You now know that the name "definition" is homonymous across conventions between: the reality, the explication of the utterance, the combination by accidents, and the indication of the quiddity. These are four distinct matters, just as the word "eye" indicates distinct matters. So learn the formulation of definition. If a name is mentioned to you and its definition is sought, then consider: if it is homonymous, seek out the meanings in which the sharing occurs. If they are three, seek three definitions, for when realities differ, definitions must necessarily differ. If it is said "What is man?" — do not covet a single definition, for "man" is shared among matters: it is applied to the pupil of the eye (insān al-ʿayn), which has a definition; to the well-known human being, which has another definition; to the painted man on a wall, which has yet another definition; and to the dead man, which has another definition. For the severed male organ and the severed hand are still called "hand" and "male organ" — not in the sense by which they were originally named, for they were named thus insofar as they were instruments of seizing and instruments of intercourse. After severance, they are named thus insofar as their form has a name; and if their form were made of wood or stone, it would be given that name.

Likewise, if it is said "What is the definition of intellect (ʿaql)?" — do not covet that it be defined by a single definition, for that is madness (hawas). It is homonymous, applied to: the instinct (gharīzah) by which man is prepared to grasp necessary sciences; the sciences acquired from experience — so much so that he whom experiences have not seasoned is not called "intelligent" in this regard; he who possesses dignity, awe, and tranquility in his sitting and speech — this being an expression of calm (hudūʾ), so it is said "So-and-so is intelligent," meaning there is calm in him; and it may be applied to him who joins action to knowledge — so much so that a horse, though at the utmost degree of sagacity, is prevented from being called "intelligent." Al-Ḥajjāj is called "intelligent" — nay, a genius (dāhiyah) — while an unbeliever, even if he excels in various medical and geometrical sciences, is not called "intelligent" but rather either a genius or an excellent man. Thus do conventions differ, and it is necessarily incumbent that definitions multiply in the definition of intellect. By one of its referents, it is: some of the necessary sciences concerning the possibility of the possible and the impossibility of the impossible. By the second consideration, it is: an instinct by which one is prepared for reflection upon the intelligibles. And so on for the remaining considerations.

If you say: "But I see people differing over definitions, and this discourse almost renders disagreement impossible. Do you then claim that the disputants are not intelligent?" — Know that disagreement over definition is conceivable in two places. The first: that the utterance be from the Book of God, the Sunnah of His Messenger, or the saying of an Imam, and that utterance be homonymous, so that contention occurs over what He meant by it. In that case, convergence upon the speaker's intent has occurred, and divergence occurs after convergence — so the disagreement is a divergence after convergence. Hence there is no dispute between him who says "the heaven is eternal" and him who says "the usurped object is guaranteed," for there is no convergence. If the word "definition" were from the Book of God or the book of an Imam, contention over its intent would be permissible, and clarifying that would belong to the craft of exegesis (tafsīr), not to the craft of rational reflection (naẓar bi-al-ʿaql). The second: that disagreement occurs in another matter in a verified manner, and the thing whose definition is sought is distinct, and its definition is not given according to the two schools, so they differ. For example, the Muʿtazilite says: "The definition of knowledge is the belief (iʿtiqād) of the thing," and we oppose him in the mention of "thing," for the non-existent (maʿdūm) is not, in our view, a "thing." So the disagreement is in another matter that extends to the definition. Likewise, one says: "The definition of intellect is some of the necessary sciences in such-and-such a manner," and he opposes him who defines it as "an instinct by which one is prepared to grasp the intelligibles," insofar as the latter denies the existence of anything else — rather, he says: "There is nothing in man but a body, in which there is life and necessary sciences, either instinctive or acquired, and theoretical sciences; the heart is not thereby distinguished from the heel, nor man from the fly, for God is able to create theoretical sciences in the heel and in the fly." Thus a disagreement in something other than the definition stirs a disagreement in the definition. This, though we have brought it in the guise of an examination, has benefited you with what runs, upon verification, in the course of principles (qawānīn).

I say: The Second Examination. They differed over the definition of knowledge (ʿilm). It was said: "It is cognition (maʿrifah)." This is a verbal definition, and it is the weakest of the kinds of definitions, for it is a repetition of the word by mentioning its synonym — as when one says the definition of motion is "transference" (nuqlah). Nor does it exit from being verbal by saying "cognition of the known as it is," for this is in the manner of prolongation and repetition, since "cognition" is only applied to that which is so. It is like one who says: "The definition of the existent is the thing that has fixity and existence" — for this prolongation does not remove it from being verbal. I do not forbid that this be called a definition, for the word "definition" in the language means "prevention," and it is permissible (mubāḥ); whoever wishes may use it metaphorically for anything containing a kind of prevention. If someone called a cap (qalansuwah) a "definition" because it prevents cold, he would not be prevented from this — if "definition" in his view is an expression for a preventive utterance. But if in his view it is an expression for a statement explicating the quiddity of a thing, imaging the very reality of it in the mind of the questioner, then he has wronged by applying this name to his saying "knowledge is cognition."

It was also said: "It is that by which one knows (mā yuʿlam bih)," and "that by which the essence becomes knowing." This definition is further from the first, for it equals it in being devoid of explication and indication of the quiddity. However, one might imagine in the first a verbal explication, in that one of the two words is more famous to the questioner than the other, so the less known is explicated by the more known. But "knower" (ʿālim) and "knowing" (yaʿlam) are derived from the very same root as knowledge itself. If the infinitive (maṣdar) is obscure to him, how should the derived form become clear to him? The derived is more obscure than that from which it is derived. This is like one who says in defining silver: "It is that from which silver vessels are fashioned."

It was also said: "It is the attribute (waṣf) by which the one described attains mastery (itqān) of knowledge and its solidification (iḥkām)." This mentions one of the necessary concomitants (lawāzim) of knowledge, making it a descriptive definition (rasmī). This one is further from the mark in one respect, for it is more specific than knowledge, since it applies to some sciences only. But it is closer in another respect than what preceded it, for it mentions a necessary concomitant close to the essence, remote from explication and clarification — unlike his saying "that by which one knows" and "that by which the essence becomes knowing."

If you say: "What then is your way of defining knowledge?" — Know that knowledge is a homonymous name. It may be applied to vision (ibṣār) and sensation (iḥsās), and it has a definition accordingly; it is applied to imagination (takhayyul), and it has another definition accordingly; it is applied to opinion (ẓann), and it has another definition accordingly; it is applied to God's knowledge in yet another manner, higher and nobler — and I do not mean nobler merely by virtue of generality alone, but by essence and reality. And it is applied to the intellect's apprehension (idrāk al-ʿaql) alone, as presently strikes the mind: that it is the soul's stillness (sukūn al-dhihn) with certainty (jazm), upon insight (baṣīrah), concerning a matter being thus or not thus, while the matter is indeed so. It is not unlikely that this definition requires further refinement and polishing, but the heart does not now have room to waste time on it. So it is upon you to complete it. My purpose is to mention the way of definition.

You say: "They object to this definition by noting that you used the word 'stillness' (sukūn), which is homonymous; 'mind' (dhihn), which is obscure; and 'insight' (baṣīrah), which seems to indicate connection." — But pay no heed to those infatuated with expressions, who are turned away from realities by other than the truth. Know that "stillness," when conjoined with "mind," loses its ambiguity; and I mentioned "mind" because I suppose it is understood by you — and I do not forbid substituting it for one who does not know it. For the purpose of the real definition is to image the very reality of the quiddity in the soul of the one seeking to benefit, by whatever utterance it may be.

If you say: "Is it conceivable that a single thing have two definitions?" — I say: As for the verbal definition, it is conceivable that it have a thousand, varying with the abundance of names in some languages and their scarcity in others, and varying across nations. As for the descriptive definition, it too may multiply, for the necessary concomitants of things are not limited. As for the real definition, it is conceivable only as one, for the essential attributes (dhātiyyāt) are limited. If one does not mention them, it is not real; if one mentions some of them, the definition is deficient; and if one mentions, along with the essential attributes, an addition, the addition is superfluous (ḥashw). Thus this definition does not multiply.

I say: The Third Examination. It was said in the definition of accident (ʿaraḍ): "That which does not endure," or "that whose endurance is impossible," or "that which does not subsist by itself." This is defective, for it mentions a necessary concomitant without attending to the essence; moreover, it is a negative concomitant, whereas affirmation is closer to making understood. It was also said: "It is that which inheres in substance (jawhar)." Your saying "inheres" (yaʿriḍ) seems to be derived from "accident" itself, and it introduces substance into its definition — substance being also something whose definition is sought, which could be referred back to accident by saying "that in which the accident subsists." So this art is not satisfactory. Rather, we say: The seeker of this definition is as if he seeks to understand what we mean by this name in our convention. Otherwise, accident is that whose reality is established in the soul with a primary establishment (thubūt awwalī) that does not require seeking it through the craft of definition — for we have established that some cognitions are dispensed from definition in their comprehension; otherwise, the matter would regress infinitely.

So we say to him: Know that the intellect apprehended existence (wujūd), then apprehended its division into that which requires a locus (maḥall) in which it subsists, and that which does not require it. Then it apprehended the division of that which subsists in the locus into that which supervenes after not having been, and that which is not supervening — like the attributes of God Most High. Thus "accident" is an expression for that which supervenes after not having been, and its definition requires, at the time, that it be an originated thing (ḥādith) whose existence requires a locus in which it subsists. As for the Muʿtazilites, since they deny the attributes of the Creator, their convention does not require the restriction to the originated; rather, they may express by it every existent that subsists in another.

I say: The Fourth Examination. It was said in the definition of the originated (ḥādith): "That which is not eternal (qadīm)." This is madness, like one who says: "The eternal is that which is not originated" — for it is defining one opposite by the other, and the matter turns in a circle. It was also said: "It is that to which eternal power (al-qudrah al-qadīmah) is attached." This mentions an obscure necessary concomitant, grasped only through proofs. But the originated is a clear concept (mafhūm jalī) without reflection and inference; and it is from far error to clarify the clear by the obscure. By my life, whoever applies the name "definition" to every comprehensive preventive utterance — then this is, for him, undoubtedly a definition, as is his saying "the originated is that which is not eternal." But we say: The intellect apprehended existence, then apprehended its division into that which has a beginning — meaning it was not existent then became existent — and that which has no beginning. The eternal is an expression for one of the two divisions, and the originated for the other. So we say: The originated is "the existent after non-existence" (al-mawjūd baʿd al-ʿadam), or "the coming-to-be after not having been" (al-kāʾin baʿd an lam yakun), or "the existent preceded by non-existence" (al-mawjūd al-masbūq bi-ʿadam), or "the existent from non-existence" (al-mawjūd ʿan ʿadam). These are not multiple definitions; rather, all are one definition with repeated expressions, not repeated meanings. Not like one who says: "It is that to which originated power is attached," for that is another definition whose primary concept is other than the concept of these definitions, though that concept entails it — for the object of power's attachment entails that it be originated. And there is a difference between two mutually entailing things (mutalāzimayn) and a single thing expressed by two expressions.

As for one's saying "the existent from non-existence" — this is not sound, for one says "the bed is from wood," meaning that wood was made into a bed; but non-existence does not make existence. This is a matter of rare objections. For we do not deny that the word "from" (ʿan) is homonymous; but we have shown that a homonym, when understood by context (qarīnah), attains the status of the unambiguous (naṣṣ) — and this is known here. I do not forbid striving to avoid the homonym, for that is better; I only forbid magnifying this practice, which is not magnified by the accomplished scholar. Neither is this blameworthy with all that blame after understanding is achieved, nor is that praiseworthy with all that praise — especially when it does not benefit the explication. Rather, the matter is easier than what is supposed. Indeed, one's saying "existent from non-existence" is more beloved to me than his saying "it is the object of power's attachment."

I say: The Fifth Examination. They differed over the definition of the two contraries (mutadāddān). My purpose is not merely the definitions, but rather to benefit you with the way of definition after having established it in the preceding. So let your consideration of definitions be as I say: The two contraries necessarily indicate two things. Every two things divide into those having a locus and those having no locus. Everything having a locus divides into what can coexist — like blackness and motion — and what cannot coexist. That which cannot coexist divides into what differs in definition and reality — like blackness and whiteness — and what does not differ. That which does not differ also divides into what cannot be such that one of them is an accident or necessary concomitant for one thing and not for the other; rather, one stands in the place of the other in every state — like two whitenesses and two blacknesses, in sum, like two similars (mithlān). And into what agrees in definitions and reality, whose natures do not differ, but one does not stand in the place of the other — like two "being-in" (kawn) states in two places, not like two "being-in" states in one place, for there cannot coexist in a substance in a single state neither two "being-in" states in one place nor a "being-in" in two places. That which has difference between them divides into what has the utmost difference, beyond which no difference can be — like blackness and whiteness, and ascending motion and descending motion — and into what is not at the utmost — like the difference of hot water from lukewarm, which is less than its difference from cold and intensely cold; and like the difference of rightward motion from ascending, which is less than its difference from leftward motion, I mean the opposite.

When these divisions are established in your mind, then look at the word "two contraries" and how the convention has been placed upon it. The lowest degree of the two contraries are the two meanings that alternate upon a single locus and do not coexist — whether they are different or similar. One group has agreed to apply the name to this, so they call two similars "contraries." Another group stipulated an addition for applying this name: that one does not stand in the place of the other — so they did not apply it to two "being-in" states in one locus, but applied it to two "being-in" states in two loci. A third group stipulated an additional matter: that there be between them a difference in definition and reality — i.e., one does not enter into the definition of the other. For when we define "being-in" (kawn) as "appropriation of a locus" (ikhtiṣāṣ bi-al-ḥayyiz), all "being-in" states enter into it; there is no difference by nature between loci, nor between "being-in" states — they are similar. So these did not call the "being-in" states contraries, but rather the differing things like heat and cold. A fourth group stipulated an addition: that there be between them the utmost difference possible in that kind of contrariety, such that no difference lies beyond it. These are the philosophers, and this is their convention. They claimed that whiteness is not contrary to the woody, but to blackness; and heat is not contrary to lukewarm, but to cold. This is the explication.

We see a group of the blind (ʿumyān) wrangling over these definitions, supposing there is contention in them, not realizing that reflection is of two kinds: one is over bare realities without regard to utterances — and these are the divisions we first mentioned, none of which any intelligent person denies; the second is over the application of utterances and conventions — and this pertains to the conventional (waḍʿī). For utterances are abundant and permissible; no restriction from the Law has fixed them upon a specific meaning such that their use in another manner is forbidden. By my life, if it were said that the coiner of language coined it for something originally, then it is restricted to it in reality, and for other than it is a metaphor (istiʿārah) — this I do not deny. But delving into this befits not the accomplished scholar who reflects upon intelligibles, but rather the men of letters who examine languages. You may see one who becomes incensed and says: "How does an intelligent man permit himself to say that two 'being-in' states are not contraries, when it is known that they do not coexist?" This is only due to a false syllogism in his soul of which he is unaware. The arrangement of that syllogism is: Our saying "they are contraries" and our saying "they do not coexist" are one and the same. So how can it be said "they coexist" and "they do not coexist"? For it appears that everything that does not coexist must necessarily be called "contraries," and it is known that two "being-in" states do not coexist, so they must be called "contraries." But who knows that the necessity of naming what does not coexist "contraries" is not established? Rather, naming belongs to the people of convention.

I say: The Sixth Examination. It was said in the definition of life (ḥayāh): "It is the meaning (maʿnā) by which he who is described by it deserves that the name 'living' (ḥayy) be derived for him from it." This is among the weakest of definitions, for it defines the meaning by an utterance applied to the meaning. He who is satisfied with this in understanding life has been satisfied, from the sciences, with their husks (qushūr). It was also said: "That which necessitates the living being's being living," or "that by which the locus is living." You have already known what is in this genus. It was also said: "That by whose existence knowledge becomes sound," or "that by whose existence power or will becomes sound." This is defining the thing by mentioning some of its consequents.

If you say: "What is your choice in this?" — Know that mentioning that is not borne by this book. For here there is a consideration of utterances — which are three: life (ḥayāh), spirit (rūḥ), and soul (nafs) — and a consideration of meanings and realities. Among people, there is he who says: "There is nothing in man but life, which is an accident subsisting in his body, and the names 'soul' and 'spirit' revert to it." Among them is he who says: "There must be, besides this accident, a thing that is the spirit — a subtle body (jism laṭīf) within the heart and brain, flowing to the rest of the body through the pulsating veins. As for the soul, it has no third referent." Among them is he who says: "Here there is a third matter — an existent subsisting by itself, not occupying space (ghayr mutaḥayyiz); and the spirit, which is the subtle body whose source is the heart, directs the other organs of the body by its mediation." Observe how the path differed for them, and how the difference is witnessed! For I shall alert you to its beginnings, though the book cannot bear delving into its depths.

Know that when the inquirer looked at the sperm-drop (nuṭfah), which is inanimate (jamād), neither sensing nor moving, then it transformed through the stages of creation until it came to sense and move — he knew that there occurred in it what had not been, namely sensation and voluntary motion. He supposed that there is nothing in this existence but the body: it was inanimate, then God created in it sensation and the power of motion. So nothing was added but power and sensation, and at that point it is called "living," and this name is renewed for it. Thus life was an expression for sensation and power alone. When he looked at the languages, he saw this fetus and this man in the state of apoplexy (saktah) called "living," and the name applied truly to him. He conjectured in himself, by apparent imagination (wahm) before verification by proof, that this man in his apoplexy has no sensation at all nor power. So he sought a referent for it and supposed that there is nothing here but the possibility of creating sensation in him and creating power — so he is called "living" insofar as he is prepared to receive it, and life is an expression for preparedness (istiʿdād) alone. But it had settled in his belief that God is able to create life in every body, and God is not described as having power to create sensation and motion in the inanimate. So it occurred to him that there must be an attribute by which the one in apoplexy is distinguished from the inanimate, such that the creation of sensation and power in him is conceivable by virtue of it, unlike the inanimate. So he said: "Life is an expression for that attribute," and he affirmed for him an attribute that is life. Among them is he who was satisfied with this consideration and supposed in himself that there is no existent but the body and an attribute by which the locus is prepared to receive sensation and power. Among them is he who went beyond this and was led by the craft of medicine, and by being content with it, to religious matters from the craft of medicine. For it indicated that the four humors produce a subtle vapor of extreme subtlety: in the heart there is an innate heat (ḥarārah gharīziyyah) that cooks that vapor, subtilizes it, and dispatches it — a power in the heart through the cavities of the pulsating veins to the rest of the body. The sensitive power reaches the eye, ear, and the other five senses through this subtle vapor coursing with its subtlety through the channels of the nerves. So this vapor is the carrier of these powers, running in the thread of the veins and supplying the subtle bodies in which the powers of sensation reside. They said: "If a blockage occurred in some of the passages of this vapor — either in a nerve or a vein — life and sensation would cease in that which the blockage separated from the heart, until its supply was cut off." So they expressed this subtle air as "spirit" (rūḥ) and claimed it is the cause of the continuance of life in the individual organs. Thus it was established for them that there is a subtle body, which they expressed as "spirit," and they judged that it is the cause of the accident called "life."

As for their turning to the Law: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: {«أرواح الشهداء في حواصل طيور معلقة تحت العرش»} ("The souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds suspended beneath the Throne"). And His saying, Most High: {«ولا تحسبن الذين قتلوا في سبيل الله أمواتا بل أحياء عند ربهم يرزقون»} ("Do not reckon those killed in the path of God as dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord, provided for"). So they claimed: "There was nothing but life, which is an accident, and it has been annihilated by death, while the corpse of the dead is before us. What then is in the crops of green birds? And how are the martyrs described as alive when the body we witness is dead, and life is an accident that has been annihilated?" Likewise, they turned to his saying ﷺ in his supplication upon sleeping: {«إن أمسكتها فاغفر لها وإن أرسلتها فاعصمها بما تعصم به عبادك الصالحين»} ("If You take it, then forgive it; and if You send it back, then protect it as You protect Your righteous servants"). They said: "What is it that is taken and sent back? The body is present, and life is an accident that cannot be sent." They also turned to His saying, Most High: {«ويسألونك عن الروح قل الروح من أمر ربي»} ("And they ask you about the spirit. Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord"). Why did He not tell them that it is an accident, like power and life, if there is nothing here but body and accident?

At this point a third group arose and delved deeper, saying: "This is sound, but this spirit is in his body. There is another existent expressed as 'soul' (nafs), whose attribute is that it subsists by itself, not occupying space; its relation to the body is like God's relation to the world — neither inside it nor outside it." They turned to the fact that the spirit is a divisible body whose parts are similar. If it were the director and perceiver in man, then each person would have many spirits, and it would be possible that some of its parts have knowledge of a thing while others have ignorance of it — so it would be knowing of a thing and ignorant of it. Therefore, there must be something that penetrates without dividing, and every body is divisible. They claimed that the indivisible body is impossible. Then they turned, with that, to how this spirit is sent or held in the state of sleep. If the spirit left the body in sleep, he would be dead, not alive. And since imaginations, dreams, and knowledge of the unseen by way of true visions are sound, they claimed that nothing departs from the sleeper that separates from him — for if it returned to him, it would enter through an aperture, and bodies do not interpenetrate. And if one bound the sleeper's mouth and nose first, then woke him, he would wake. They observed in it other matters that cannot be enumerated, and

chapters.arabic_text:
### | خاتمة الكتاب

ثم ألحق به أن قال اعلم أن القدر الذي حررته في هذا الكتاب مع صغر حجمه
حركت به أصولا عظيمة إن أمعنت في تفهم الكتاب تشرفت إلى مزيد إيضاح في بعض
ما أجملته واشتغلت لحكم الحال عن تفصيله، وذلك التفصيل قد أودعت بعضه كتاب
معيار العلوم. إلا أنني لم أفش تلك النسخة ولم تتداولها إلا يدي بعد، لأنها
كانت مفتقرة إلى مزيد تهذيب وتنقيح بحذف وزيادة  وتحريف، وفد دفعت الأقدار
دون تهذيبها فإن استأخر الأجل واندفعت العوائق وانصرفت إليه الهمة وانقطعت
على عمارته بتهذيب ما يجب أن يهذب صادفت فيه ما أعوزك ني هذا الكتاب. وأنا
الآن مجدد وصيتك بالمواظبة على الدعاء سائلا من الله تعالى أن يصلح نيتي
فيما أتعاطاه من تصنيف كتاب وإفادة علم لأقصد به خالص وجه الله غير ممزوج
بحظ من حظوظ الدنيا، وما أخس حال من مهد للخلق سبيل الآخرة وهو إلى الدنيا
ملتفت، أو - دعا الخلق إلى الله وهو عنه معرض. فنعوذ بالله من شرور أنفسنا
وسيئات أعمالنا ونسأل الله تعالى إصلاح أحوالنا وأقوالنا وأفعالنا، فهو ولي
الإجابة بفضله وسعة جوده والحمد لله رب العالمين. PageV01P279
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ختم (khatama)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To seal, conclude, or stamp; the final closure of a thing, marking its completion and fixed end.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, the sealing of a matter signifies its definitive termination, often tied to divine decree or the consummation of an act of worship or knowledge.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (Ḥaqīqah) — the physical stamping of a seal; metaphorical (Majāz) — the closing of a discourse or book, as here, where the seal is the author’s final address.
- Sībawayh Rule: Inna wa akhawātuhā (Verbs of Certainty) — The opening «اعلم أن» governs a nominal clause, establishing a definitive epistemic assertion; the subsequent conditional clauses (إن أمعنت...) are syntactically dependent on this, creating a protasis-apodosis structure that requires careful nesting in translation.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the measure which I have set down in this book, despite its small size, has set in motion mighty principles. If you ponder deeply the understanding of the book, you will be elevated toward further elucidation of some of what I have summarized, and you will occupy yourself, due to the exigency of the present circumstance, with what I have left undetailed. That detailing I have deposited partly in the book *The Criterion of the Sciences* (Miʿyār al-ʿUlūm). However, I have not divulged that copy, nor has it been circulated beyond my own hand as yet, because it stood in need of further polishing and refinement — by deletion, addition, and emendation. The decrees of fate have hindered its refinement. If the term of life is deferred, obstacles are repelled, resolve turns toward it, and one devotes oneself to its completion by refining what must be refined, you will find therein what has eluded you in this book.

And now I renew my charge to you: persist in supplication, asking God Most High to rectify my intention in what I undertake — the composition of books and the imparting of knowledge — so that I aim thereby solely at the pure face of God, unmixed with any share of worldly gains. How base is the state of one who paves for creation the path to the Hereafter while he himself is turned toward this world, or who calls people to God while he is himself averse to Him! We seek refuge in God from the evils of our souls and the misdeeds of our works, and we ask God Most High to rectify our states, our words, and our deeds. For He is the Guardian of answering, by His bounty and the vastness of His generosity. And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.
